speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RESIGNATION OF MR. WALTER G. MITCHELL
speechtext:
I see by the press that
Mr. Walter Mitchell is desirous of having his letter to me regarded as a public one. While I do not know that it is customary to place on the Table correspondence respecting the resignations of private members, nevertheless I feel that hon. members of the House might wish to see a copy of Mr. Mitchell's letter and my reply thereto. I therefore beg to lay these letters on the Table of the House.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 116, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
He said:	The purpose of this bill is to
widen the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court to deal with matters which might be submitted to it after an arrangement or agreement between the Crown and other parties.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Does the hon. minister
mean between the Crown and another party to an action in the court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose is to widen the jurisdiction of the court, so that the Crown could submit to the Exchequer Court any other question which is not already under
their jurisdiction, provided the other party agrees to it.

Would the other party
require to be a party of the action in the court before he could agree to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 117, to amend the Expropriation Act.
He said:	The purpose of this amendment
is to enable the government or contractors to carry out blasting operations which may be necessary in connection with the execution of any public work without proceeding to expropriate. At present the Crown must expropriate the whole property, while it may be possible that the damages are not of such a nature as to warrant expropriation. Under this measure we will pay the damages and proceed with the blasting operations.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

LAUSANNE TREATY On the Orders of the Day:
Is the Prime Minister in a position to lay on the Table of the House the correspondence with regard to the Lausanne Treaty or to make any statement thereon?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: (Prime Minister): It had been my intention to suggest this evening that to-morrow we take up a consideration of the Lausanne matter. I have, however, received within the last few hours, a cable from the British government to which I have replied. Pending further possible word I think it would be well, perhaps, to allow the discussion to stand until Wednesday that I may have the correspondence with the British government complete.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
After the correspondence is on the Table in full, it would be unfair to bring the discussion on immediately. Certainly the House would want an opportunity to read the correspondence and to see if some light or clear line of action can be deduced from it. I suggest that unless the correspondence is laid on the Table to-day, it would be unfair to bring the discussion on so soon as Wednesday.
TMr. Coote.]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I agree with my right hon. friend. I may say that the government has not yet obtained the consent of the British government to lay the correspondence on the Table, but I hope it will foe possible to get that consent, and it is in .that hope that I still am waiting. If this consent is obtained I shall be pleased to allow whatever time hon. members may wish for the purpose of reading the correspondence in the first instance. That, I think, would be the quickest way of disposing of the whole matter.
Has the Prime Minister yet received replies to those telegrams which were despatched some weeks ago to the-other dominions in order to ascertain which was the recalcitrant dominion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have the
answers here and I may as well take this occasion to read them to the House. On May 6 I sent a message to the Prime Ministers, respectively, of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland; I did not include the Irish Free State as I understood that it had not been organized at the time the Lausanne Conference was being arranged. The message I cabled to Australia was as follows:
Ottawa, May 6, 1924.
Premier Bruce,
Melbourne, Australia.
Canadian government desires to have tabled in Great Britain and Canada correspondence between Canada and Great Britain respecting Lausanne Conference and invitations thereto. Cable despatches state Secretary of State for Colonies says Imperial government does not object but that by agreement at Imperial Conference consent of all dominions should first be obtained. Please advise by cable if government of Australia is agreeable to having tabled such correspondence between Canada and Great Britain as may be agreed upon by British and Canadian governments.
Mackenzie King.
Premier Bruce, of Australia, replied on May 7:
Your telegram dated 6th May Lausanne Conference. Commonwealth government has no objection tabling correspondence .between Canada and Great Britain Have however already advised British government that so far as Australia is concerned prior to making of any statement purporting to summarize the views of the Dominions on this question the desirability that such statement be communicated to us prior to publicity.
A cable, in words identical to that sent Australia, was sent to the other dominions.
On May 12 General Smuts, the Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa, cabled:
Your telegram dated 6th May: I have not seen the correspondence but I raise no objection to publication.

Supply-Labour
Referring your telegram May 6: Government Newfoundland is agreeable to having tabled such correspondence between Canada and, Great Britain as may be agreed upon by British and Canadian governments respecting Lausanne Conference and invitations thereto.
On May 11 Premier Massey, of New Zealand, replied:
Your telegram sixth Understand communications mentioned were not written with view to publication and if made public am afraid would interfere with clear and frank information being given Dominions to which they are undoubtedly entitled.
I cannot say whether that last message is intended to imply that the correspondence should not be brought down. If it is not so intended, it. would appear that all the dominions were agreeable to having the correspondence tabled. I should observe however that *the Secretary of State for the Colonies in a despatch to me referring to the press despatch which had appeared regarding his answer in the House of Commons, intimated that the despatch which we received from the press here was not wholly in accord with the answer he had made in the House of Commons. I expect to get word to-day some time, or tomorrow, as to whether the British government will be agreeable to the whole of the correspondence being brought down or not.
Mr. ME1GHEN: Will the Prime Minister say what is the significance of the words "such as may be agreed upon between the British government and the Canadian government" appearing at the end of his own message to the dominions and re-echoed in. the reply of at least one, the Prime Minister of Newfoundland? These words imply that all that is suggested by the Prime Minister of Canada is that only such correspondence shall be brought down as shall be later agreed upon between the governments. If so, the agree-.ment to bring down correspondence amounts to nothing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The purport of these words is that our government would like to have all the correspondence brought down. The British government, however, may object to all of it being brought down, and in that event we should like to have submitted as much as they will agree to. That is the significance of the sentence.

necessary to deal with some of the conditions and some of the reports that my hon. friend refers to. Under the British North America Act, as I have said before, and as my hon. friend possibly knows better than I do, the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over property and civil rights; and therefore in regard to very many of these questions that my hon. friend naturally brings before parliament and the federal Labour department, and asks to have them dealt with, or asks, "What are you doing about it?"-we have not any authority to act except by conciliation, or by an indication of our readiness to do anything we have authority to do, or that we are capable of doing. I would then assure him that the Labour department would move in the direction indicated by him if there was not a blind end to the lane he starts us down.

I will tell the minister
how to go about the matter. He might just take the matter up with his friends in the Nova Scotia government. They have authority to change conditions down in Sydney. Has the minister made any representations to the Nova Scotia government in regard to the matter? While he is thinking that over, I should like to ask him this further question:	What steps, if any, did he or the officers of his department take to bring about any change in conditions down there, and what, if anything, did they do to settle the difficulties in Nova Scotia before the troops were sent there?
In 1923, the steel workers asked for a board of investigation. We did the best that the Labour department could do to get that board of investigation for them, but it was impossible to do so.
Why?

In the first place the
dispute was in a private industrial concern over which it has never been held that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act has jurisdiction.
That is to say, the company did not yield to the representations.

Although section 63 of
the act gives permission, of course, to the minister to establish a board where the two parties agree to have a board, in this case the steel workers made an application for a board; we tried to get the agreement of the company to establish a board, but they declined. That made a situation where we seemed to be powerless to do anything further. There was no law or authority under which we could act further. We went along until June when the steel workers made other requests and finally went on strike, later getting the mine workers with them, and with the result, still later, that the troops were called out. At every stage where there seemed reasonable opportunity for us to do or to offer to do anything, we did what appeared possible, but my hon. friend will realize how .powerless is any one who has not authority, to do something. All he can do is to offer his friendly offices or the friendly offices of his department, and this was done in every case as opportunity presented itself.

I suppose the Department of Labour had something to do with the thousands of men who were sent out west to help in the harvest of last year. Absolutely no suggestion whatsoever was made, with any authority, by any one in the department as to what wages were to be paid. My hon. friend will remember that eleven thousand or twelve thousand of the harvesters last year came direct from overseas, going to the West, and with these the Department of Labour had nothing to do. The department however, did cooperate with the employment service and with the railways, as it has done in former years, in the recruiting of unemployed labour in the eastern provinces and sending it forward for service in the West. That was not the case in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, who had a good deal to do with bringing men from Great Britain.
I can say nothing so far as that is concerned.
Does my hon. friend object to the labour brought into western Canada last year to move the crop?

I object to unskilled men being brought from Great Britain on the strength of the promise that they will be paid the wages of skilled men, although they know nothing about the work which they are going to undertake.

We have made no such promise.
fMr. Murdock.]

There are a great many labourers in the Maritime provinces who go west during the harvest. They do not complain about the wages, which they consider fair; but the hours of labour they think are too long: they are required to work from twelve to fifteen hours a day and sometimes as long as seventeen hours. That is something which I should like my western friends to take into consideration.
I challenge that statement, so far as Manitoba is concerned.

I have had it directly
from men who have gone west and have returned to my constituency; I could give their names.
As an old Manitoban I can say that the hours of labour during harvest time in that province are from 7 a.m. to 12 noon, and from 1 p.m. to 6 and, on some farms, 7 o'clock.
They are not as bad in Manitoba as they are in other places in the West.

I wish to follow this question up a little further. I have personal experience in this matter, having frequently gone down to the railway for a number of years to meet harvest excursion trains. Every year I am accosted with the statement that these men have been promised $4, $4.50 and even $5 a day, and what my hon. friend (Mr. Spencer) is no doubt trying to find out is the source from which this information comes. It is useless trying to engage these men at any lower wage. It is quite true that a good many of them are worth the money; but going on a train and looking over four or five hundred men who are going west in search of work one can invariably pick out the competent man. But the trouble is that the incompetent man will repeat with gusto the same story in regard to these promised wages, and ft seems to me, from a long experience, that as these harvesters are all armed with this promise or alleged promise, it would be just as well to trace the origin of the information which apparently is given them in the first instance. If the Department of Labour does not make any definite statements to them, the question is, does it convey by implication any promise that these men will receive a certain wage if they go west? The Minister ptated something about employers getting together in the case of the Welland canal, for instance, and suggesting 40 cents or 45 cents to be paid. The committee will realise that .the farmers are unable to get together to arrange a definite rate of wages. I believe

Supply-Labour
that if the department would co-operate with certain farmers' organizations it might be possible to arrive at some definite rate, or to come to some understanding, that would be equitable to all concerned.

My hon. friend forgets that the provinces are really in closer touch with the employment service in the various parts of the Dominion than is the federal government. All that the federal government does is to co-operate with the provinces in maintaining a chain of employment offices clear across Canada. There are provincial employees in all these offices, but we have at Winnipeg one superintendent and two other employees who staff what is called a clearing house to keep in touch with the western territory. That is all the connection we have with the service in that particular regard. My hon. friend asked whether we suggested the wages to be paid. When labour is to be recruited in the East the labour offices in that part of the country indicate what wages the farmers are offering, and that information is given to the prospective employee in the east. We only act or intend to act as a messenger or go-between.
It seems, then, that the abstract becomes the concrete when these men go west, and that the general idea as to what is being offered in the West is construed as a definite promise.

Item agreed to.
Administration, Employment Offices, Co-ordination Act, $50,000.
There is an increase of $20,000.

We have, I think,
really three departments that have to do with employment, namely, the Labour department, the Immigration department and the department that has charge of the settlement of soldiers. Will the minister give us a statement regarding the relations that exist among these three departments, and the measure of co-operation that is practised?

The Soldier Settlement
Board is under the Department of Immigration. This particular vote contemplates an increase of $20,000 as indicated by my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton). The intention is to take from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment the employment service activities that have been handled in certain large cities of Canada for handicapped exservice men and to co-ordinate that service with and handle it in the present employment offices, with possibly some additional staff 145
where necessary, to be paid out of this vote, the federal government paying 100 per cent. This vote, and it is an increase of $20,000, contemplates a co-ordination of existing employment services, that is, coupling up the D.S.C.R. employment service for handicapped ex-service men and the general employment service of the federal and provincial governments. The Soldier Settlement Board employment service is under the Immigration department.

It is in regard to that that I want a little clearer light. When the twelve thousand harvesters came over from Great Britain last year was there a consultation between the Immigration department and the Labour department before the campaign was started?

Generally fairly close
touch has been maintained between the Immigration department and the Labour department. Usually, if not always, when additional help is requested from various concerns or individuals the Immigration department ascertain from the Labour department if the Employment Service of Canada is able to furnish the help required, and only in the event of being advised that the help is not available do the Immigration department give permission for this additional labour to come forward. My hon. friend will recall that last year we had in prospect one of the biggest crops in the history of western Canada. It was rather difficult to determine accurately the approximate number of labourers required to handle that crop. It might be said that possibly there was not that collaboration between the Immigration department, the Employment Service of Canada and other bodies which there might have been if we had known beforehand exactly how many men Alberta or Saskatchewan or Manitoba needed. But we could not take a chance of failing to meet the requirements of the West and we had to start to get labour from the East and, to a considerable extent, from overseas in order to be sure of a full supply. As a result I can appreciate my hon. friend may say that we might have known some things that under the circumstances it was impossible for us to know.

I understand the
Labour department has been doing rather good work in trying to dovetail seasonal employment. For example, at certain seasons it is becoming customary for workers in British Columbia to be brought over the mountains to the prairies. Last year that arrangement was more or less disturbed. Then there was a great scurrying around by the Soldier Settle-

ment Board-I happened to be in Alberta in the autumn and observed it-which sent its agents all over the country trying to place newly arrived Old Country immigrants. This of course meant that British Columbia and other Canadian workmen were replaced by newer arrivals. Has the minister any information on this particular point?

I do not know that I quite get my hon. friend's question. I can assure him that by co-operation and co-ordination we hope to prevent any conflict of effort that may have occurred in the past. This particular vote is to bring about coordination that we think will be valuable and effective. Possibly later further co-ordination can be brought about that will also be valuable.

I asked about a particular matter last year. We had the Soldier Settlement Board sending officials all over the country to find places for some of these Old Country immigrants, and I understand that this resulted in upsetting more or less the arrangements which the employment office had been building up by which men were brought in from British Columbia to work in the western part of the prairie provinces.

My hon. friend is correct. It was alleged that to a certain extent there was that condition. But he must not overlook the fact that about twelve thousand immigrants came from overseas to help gather the western harvest. The Soldier Settlement Board and the Department of Immigration were naturally keeping in close touch with those immigrants and doing everything possible to secure them employment after the harvesting operations were completed. In doing so there was possibly some little conflict, which it is hoped may not recur.

Coming to this year, I have resolutions from Winnipeg, passed within the last few weeks, complaining of the hundreds of unemployed who are finding it impossible to obtain any work in that city, and that notwithstanding this serious condition of unemployment thousands of new arrivals are pouring in. So bad has this become that the city itself is protesting, and, I understand, has been making advances to other Canadian cities with a view to lodging a united protest against the dumping of immigrants who take the place of our unemployed.
I think my hon. friend should wait until the Minister of Immigration comes forward with his estimates and talk to him about that.
I will.

I appreciate the difficulty of the unemployed in the cities. When I was home at Easter I tried to get the employment service to send men out to my farm, but none have been sent along so far. We have always to take into account the fact that in Winnipeg and other cities there are men who simply will not go on the farm-and many of them are no good when they do go. I think from the standpoint of the men themselves, when large numbers are brought out to this country they should not be advised that any kind of man is going to get $5 a day in the harvest field. I have distinctly in mind cases last harvest where men came out with the impression that they were going to get that high wage. The farmers simply would not pay this rate and the men had to be sent adrift. Both from the standpoint of the farmers and the labourers themselves I think there should be great care exercised in advising men just what wages they are going to get in the harvest field, because otherwise it means disappointment all around. I realize that the whole question is a very difficult one. While naturally I am desirous of getting our wheat harvested at a price which we can afford to pay, yet I think we must be reasonable and recognize the difficulty of those who undertake to provide a supply of labour in gauging just exactly the number of harvesters required. I should like to see the fullest co-operation between the farmers' organizations, the various government departments and the railroad companies; there might even be more co-operation than there has been in the past. I would urge upon officials of the department and upon railway officials and others who promise men high wages in the harvest field to put in a qualifying clause- that the men must be such as can earn the wage that the farmers are willing to pay. There is dissatisfaction all around if that is not done.

Mr. Chairman, if I might drag this discussion back from the harvest fields of the West,-I would ask the minister what is the custom of the department on receipt of a report from one of its employment officers that in some town, we will say in Ontario, there are from forty to two hundred unemployed? What would the minister's policy be with regard to immigrants going into that town? What does he do? Does he do anything?

I do not know that it
could be handled in the way my hon. friend suggests.

I have not made any suggestion yet.

Supply-Labour

My hon. friend suggests that there might be 200 unemployed in a certain city. As a matter of fact there are more than that in Toronto all the time. Every month of the busiest year there are more than that number who, perhaps, do not want to work, who, perhaps, would not work no matter what kind of job they were offered, and Toronto is the chief point, with Montreal or Winnipeg, to which very many of the people of this country go. Therefore we do not maintain any supervision along the lines suggested by my hon. friend.

The Minister of Labour has nothing to do with the Sarnia employment office other than to see that it is conducted in accordance with an agreement between the minister and the Ontario government and to pay a proportion of the costs of operating it. Therefore the circumstances in connection with the number of employed there would be reported in the first place to the superintendent of the provincial employment service at Toronto, who would have first-hand knowledge of the conditions; then later it would go to the clearing house in Ottawa. The Department of Immigration through their own officers or through the Soldier Settlement Board are handling the immigration end of it. So my hon. friend will see that the Minister of Labour does not deal directly with the situation he speaks about.

Surely the
minister is fully aware of the movement that 145*	'
is on foot not only throughout the East but also in the West, particularly in cities like Winnipeg and Edmonton. For example, the mayor of Edmonton refused to accept a relay of immigrants from Winnipeg on the appeal of the mayor of Winnipeg, on the ground that Edmonton had its own unemployed problem and had no room for these immigrants. I would like to ask the minister if his department is going to let that condition continue, or is he going to take the matter up with the Department of Immigration and see that the flow of immigrants in this country is guided by the conditions here?

The Department of
Labour and the Department of Immigration are closely in touch with each other and in conference on these matters almost daily.

And the
problem is still in that state, in spite of the co-operation that the minister speaks of?

Conditions arise which
give occasion to the statement, "We do not want immigrants," while on the other hand we get just as insistent demands in the other direction, for immigrants.
From whom do the latter come?
From many and varied quarters, from all walks of life. My hon. friend could get that data more accurately from the Minister of Immigration when he takes up his estimates.

I understand that the Dominion government co-operates with the provincial government in maintaining employment offices. Then I notice that this item is increased this year by $20,000, and there is the further fact that the employment office at Portage la Prairie has been closed, indicating a saving there. Does the minister contemplate taking on any new work which neessitates the increasing of this vote by 820,000?

My hon. friend must
have been out when I gave the explanation of this vote. It has nothing to do with the office at Portage la Prairie. The additional amount is provided to take over the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment employment service for handicapped ex-service men, the Department of Labour to make arrangements with the provincial governments to handle that work in connection with the existing employment offices, and, where necessary, to appoint additional officers. It is to prevent duplication of effort on the part of the D.S.C.R., the Labour department and the
Supply-Labour

provincial governments, to co-ordinate the employment services and therefore to reduce the cost.

I thank the minister for
his answer. I do not want the committee to think I am kicking about the closing of the employment office at Portage la Prairie. I am not sufficiently conversant with the conditions to know whether or not it was actually a necessity. I am one of those who will not ask for anything, even for my own constituency, if I do not think it is necessary.

As I understand
it, there is to be a co-ordination of services with a view to assisting disabled ex-service men to get work. Is that the idea?

No. The D.S.C.R. has
for a number of years been maintaining a separate employment service for handicapped ex-service men. That service has been diminishing during the last two or three years until now, for example, in Ontario they have offices at Toronto, London, Hamilton, and Ottawa only. This extra amount is to take that service over and to provide for its being handled where necessary in connection with the existing employment offices.

I understand from
the last few days' discussion that the government are returning to the Liberal platform of 1919. As I recall it, that platform included some provision for unemployment insurance and other kinds of insurance that would be a benefit to the workers. Are steps being taken to provide for some measure of unemployment insurance? We may deal with this matter in a fragmentary or a spasmodic way, but we shall not really touch the root of the problem until some very definite work is done along this line. We are told that other countries are moving. Is the government even going as far as securing information as to what might be done in organizing an unemployment insurance scheme?

Of course, a great deal
of information has come to the department from time to time, and we have also a very complete statement from the British Ministry of Labour dealing with unemployment insurance, as it has been developed in England.
Can we get that?
I have not got it here, but I will bring it the next time my estimates are up.
Is farm labour classified by the department as skilled or unskilled?

I would say that it
should be skilled, but it very often is not. The labour department does not classify it either way. All the department does, through the employment service, is to suggest that experienced farm labour is required.

The hon. member for Lisgar seemed to think, when he was speaking on the question of farm labor, that the present rates were entirely too high, but he did not help the minister by saying what he thought would be a fair rate. He simply objected to $5 a day.

My objection was not to
harvest wages at all; I think the hon. member has misunderstood me. My objection was to information which is evidently given to men who come there expecting to get $5 per day, whether they are able to earn it or not, and when some of them do not know anything about farm work. Some men come to the harvest fields who are worth $5 a day, and others are not worth fifty cents, and I maintained that it was unfair, from the standpoint both of the man and the employer, that men should come there under the misapprehension that any kind of man was worth $5 a day. Unfortunately, the disposition seems to prevail not only that any man can be a farmer, but that anybody can be a competent farm hand.

I do not know whether I am in order in bringing up this question under this vote, Mr. Chairman; I just came in while my hon. friend from Lisgar was speaking, and I heard farm labour being discussed. I referred to this matter when I was speaking very early last Friday morning, and am pleased to see the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Immigration in their seats now.
The point I wish to bring up relates to the harvest excursions that are run to secure farm help for the West. I urged at that time that the Minister of Railways-he was not then in his seat-or some other responsible minister should see that one part of Canada was not robbed of harvest help to supply some other part. In my province we feel very strongly about this matter. Our farmers in the potato-growing belt have to hire their help by the season, for six or seven months. We pay them good wages in order that we shall have them when the potato harvest comes round, and you can imagine the feelings of a farmer in New Brunswick who has paid a man good wages for four months, and whom he did not need for more than half that time, but kept on just so that he would have him for the potato harvest, when he sees these

Supply-Labour
big posters advertising harvesters' excursions to the West, and his man comes in at six /clock and informs him that he is going West jn the harvest excursion to-morrow or next Monday.
What wages do you pay them?

It depends on the skill of the men. I think the point of my hon. friend from Lisgar was that one man might be worth $5 or $6 or $7 a day, and another man might not be worth his board, because he did not know anything about the work, and it would take one man to show him what to do, and he might as well do the work himself. We do not have that difficulty in New Brunswick, because our help is mostly native help, and they are familiar with the work. But we regret very much to see these excursions put on. They practically rob us of the help we have been paying for four months in order to have them with us for the harvest season. I wrote the Minister of Railways last season and urged that the Canadian National Railways should not put on excursions from points where farm help was needed worse than in any other part of Canada, because it was simply robbing us of the men w ; must have if our crop was not to go to waste, and he replied that it was a matter for the management of the railways.
That would be protection, would it not?
No, justice.
Deny these men the right to go any place in Canada?

No, but do not hold out special inducements for them to leave the farmer who has been paying them good wages for four months. It is getting labour under false pretences in many cases, too, I think. I contend that this is not a matter for the railway management. This transferring of people from one point to the other should be a matter of government policy. If you leave it to the railways, of course, they like to get the fares, although I submit they are not making very much money out of these harvest excursions. I think the government should take some stand in this matter and see to it that one part of Canada is not robbed of help to supply another. It is like robbing Peter to pay Paul, or worse.

I will give very careful thought to the question of running harvest excursions out of New Brunswick next year. Nova Scotia once asked us not to do it, and I think we asked New Brunswick whether
they wanted us to do it. But I will take into consideration the representations my hon. friend has made.
Whom did you ask in New Brunswick, and what was the reply?
I could not say without looking up the files, but in every case we take it up with responsible ministers of the government.
Before these excursions are put on?
Yes, we ask them whether they want these excursions advertised to run from their respective provinces.

Would the minister
bring down the correspondence the next time his estimates are up, showing to whom he wrote and what the reply was? If we have any responsible minister or public man in New Brunswick who will advise the running of harvest excursions from our province, the farmers would like to know who he is.
I will bring down such correspondence as we may have in the department.
We like the men from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and would be very sorry to be deprived of them.

Does the minister
exercise control over the rates on the railways?
Not at all.

I do not know what else we can infer from his last remark, that if certain provinces take exception to these excursions being run, due consideration will be given to their representations. I think the objection is a very pertinent one, and one that ought to be emphasized in this parliament. We have been accustomed for quite a number of years back to having these excursions run every fall, and to seie the men after the work is over in the West come trooping back to the older provinces with the result that in the larger cities you have a large number of unemployed who are maintained during the winter by the cities, and the impression goes abroad that there is an army of unemployed here in Canada, and this is being used in the Old Country to deter desirable people from coming here. Only a week ago, while passing through Toronto, I noticed a large gathering in front of the city hall. They were supposed to be unemployed, and they were being addressed by a man whom I noticed was sent to gaol for six months by a Toronto magistrate only a few days ago. The

Mr. Chairman, this probably is about the most important matter we have discussed this session, not even excepting the budget-because after all the budget did not make many changes. I look upon the present system of appointments to trade commission-erships as an absolute farce, and the sooner that we as business men representing the taxpayers take this matter in hand and back up the minister in his efforts the better it is going to be for Canada, and particularly for the maritime parts of Canada, west as well as east. Let me give the committee some personal experiences. I am very much interested in Canadian trade with the south, particularly from the Maritime provinces. I do not believe that we can ever build up in the Maritime provinces a great trade with central Canada on account of the excessive freight rates; but we have a market to the south of us reached by the cheapest transportation in the world, where trade is beckoning to us. Last winter I spent some time looking over the situation there. Unfortunately I was not able to go to many of the places which I most desired to visit, but I went far enough to see that the conditions should be remedied.
I went to Nassau in the Bahama islands, three hundred in number, doing a tremendous trade with the Old Country and with the United States. I called at the Royal Bank and inquired about our representative. Allow me to say just here, Mr. Chairman, that while we have been laggard in our duty as a parliament in developing Canadian export trade, we owe a great deal to the banks of this country for' going to the West India islands and to the South American countries and developing a great business and advertising Canada. This applies particularly to the Royal Bank which I think has ninety branches south of Bermuda. I inquired, as I say, for our trade commissioner in Nassau. I was told: "There used to be one, there is none now." This does not look like progress to me. I asked how we 
were represented in the Bahama islands, and was informed: By an agent away around in Kingston, Jamaica. They had never seen him, they did not know his name, but they thought he was there. Now, Mr. Chairman, having had experience of travel you can appreciate the difficulties that lie in the way of the people in Nassau dealing with a commissioner in Jamaica, because it takes four long days and-nights to get from Nassau to Kingston-it is almost as bad as going across the Atlantic. Next there is the great island of Cuba, of which my friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) has spoken. I looked at the trade returns and found that even without a trade agent-although much of this trade was worked up by the former trade agent- our trade in 1923 amounted to nearly sixteen million dollars. What could we do if we had a proper trade agent to look after our business with that country? When the railway estimates are brought forward I propose to make a few remarks with reference to the Government Mercantile Marine, so for the present I will confine my attention to the Trade and Commerce department. I inquired for our trade commissioner. I was informed: We formerly had one, but we have not got one now. We are going backwards, Sir, instead of forward in seeking trade in that southern island. We should have agents in Havana, in North Cuba and in Santiago, in South Cuba, looking after our trade with that wonderful land. The other day I was examining the trade between that country and the United States, and comparing it with our Cuban trade. Ours is simply a bagatelle. I passed by Haiti, where last year even without a trade agent we did a considerable trade. Then I proceeded along the island of San Domingo, from which last year we imported $9,600,000 worth of goods and exported over $6,000,000 worth. That was without a trade agent-no one looking after the business. Everybody tells me in that country our business could be doubled and trebled if we had some one to look after our interests. We have spent $70,000,000- in providing a. mercantile marine, and we are losing in actual operation nearly $8,000,000 annually. Yet there is an island where our ships do not even call. I went on to Kingston, Jamaica, and inquired for our trade commissioner. I was told that his office was down in a back street, but I could not find it. I looked up the main street and saw the flag of the United States clearly indicating where their agency was. Finally I went to a friend of mine, the manager of the Royal Bank and said to him: Can you tell me where the trade agency of our country is in Jamaica? He sent one of

I do not like to attack this man, because he is a creature of circumstances; it is not his fault. I am bound to say that he is doing the best he can, but any one who was with him for half a day would know that he does not know Canada.

So much for the western islands; let us now go from Bermuda out to the eastward. WThat do we find? A country in which the Royal Bank of Canada, if I mistake not, has about twenty flourishing agencies carrying on business and reporting most favourably to their head office in this country. These islands include a very large area. Four days after you leave Bermuda you get to St. Kitts; then you pass on to Antigua, Barbados, Trinidad, then away down to Demerara. But in all that country, the different parts of which can only be reached by eight days' travel from Bermuda there was only one Canadian trade agent, located in Barbados, and now that office has been closed and the minister has sent down to Trinidad an official from his department who, I believe, knows no more about the trade of the West India country than I know about a pharmacy, and that is not much. Why, if the thing is a farce down Jamaica way, in this other area to which I have referred, diown the Windward and Leeward islands, it is a double comedy. We are trying to create business; we are not only sending our Canadian merchant marine down to those islands maintaining vessels that are going up and down like chips on the water, without cargo, but we are subsidizing the Royal Mail line to the extent of nearly $400,000 annually to go into that country where we have not a single man properly qualified to secure trade for Canada.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not attacking the present minister. I am very thankful he is in his present position. We have had doctrinaires long enough in the Trade and Commerce department; we have had worn-out politicians there long enough. The department has ceased to be an asylum for men who have served their country and their party, and it is now under the control, so far as he can control it, of a man who. as all the business men of Canada know, is a first class business man, and all I ask parliament to do is to give the minister practically the same power over the great trade of that country that he would have if he were sending out his own travellers, as he does send them out from his manufactories in the city of Renfrew. One only needs to visit these countries to see the farce of the conditions I am portraying here to-night; I am not overdrawing them in the slightest respect. I had no idea before going there of the trade possibilities, but when I saw them and talked to the people there who wanted to trade with us, when I found we were not even taking the trade that was offered to us, when I found we did not have the agents there to secure the trade, I came back determined to make parliament acquainted with the condition of affairs as they exist.

I would like the minister to investigate into the salaries paid these trade commissioners and tell the House if he thinks that, with the salaries provided, he is going to get successful business men like himself to live down in a hot climate like Cuba? I think it is entirely out of the question. I think adequate salaries should be paid, andl I am satisfied that with the system which the Civil Service Commission provides proper and competent representatives can be secured if such adequate salaries are paid.

I am very much in
accord with the remarks of my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) but the reason I rise now particularly is to 'ask, why is it that, in the face of these constant complaints about the system, the government does not take its courage in its hands and propose a change? Why are we treated to these whinings every, year about the awful restraint under which they labour? They cannot govern the country, they cannot change this and cannot change that; they are tied hand and foot, chained down and helpless. Let them come to parliament and submit their policy. Deputations from boards of trade come to Ottawa, go before the Prime Minister and beg for economy, and the Prime Minister tells them, "I cannot economize; there is that awful Civil Service Commission. Look at the law which places it all in their hands. In this way I am tied hand and foot," thus leading them to believe the Civil Service Commission were dictating salaries and everything, that it was superseding parliament and that the government could not escape from its chains no matter how it struggled. But all the Prime Minister has to do, if he does not like it, is to come to parliament, take his courage in his hands and propose a change. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), with all his beneficent designs for the country, is thwarted by that hostile Civil Service Commission, and if it were not for that commission he could lift agriculture into the seventh heaven. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to-night: I cannot do anything; here is this Civil Service Act. If the government want to change the act, let them come, to parliament, take the responsibility, propose the change, and do not let us hear this whine session after session, trying to load upon someone else the responsibility that now is theirs and that they and they alone can discharge.
My right hon. friend had the courage at one time and was attempting to change the acc, but he withdrew the bill.

But I was not whining.
I came to parliament and asked for it. I submitted jt to a committee and what the committee recommended, we did. We did no more. The hon. gentlemen submitted a change to a committee; the committee brought in a report which was completely antagonistic to all their claims and complaints to-night, and still they come back and try to throw on a commission and on an act of another government the responsibility for their own failure.
I am not given to whining, but I find the conditions here and I .am simply explaining them to parliament. I am not whining about anything at all.
Propose a change.

I am not suggesting a change
to-night.

I am not rising to discuss the merits or demerits of the Civil Service Commission. I should, however, like to make one or two practical suggestions to the minister with regard to, not only the appointment of a trade commissioner to Cuba, but some other things I think he should take up for the benefit of the export trade of Canada when he is appointed. Possibly I would go a little further and urge that the minister should take this matter up himself, because I do not think a trade commissioner would have authority to do something, I would like to have done, that is, to arrange for some measure of reciprocity between Cuba and Canada. We have arranged reciprocity agreements with countries with which we do very little business. As I pointed out before, Cuba is to-day our only market for potatoes. Our ships go there loaded wTith potatoes and come back loaded with raw sugar. In view of the extremely high price of sugar at the present time, we might very well arrange for some reciprocity agreement with Cuba for a freer exchange of potatoes and sugar, because at the present time the United States has a preference over us in the duty on potatoes of 
about twelve cents a bag, which is quite an item when the margin is so very close as it is to the potato grower. I hope the minister will make a note of this, not forget it and not keep it under consideration too long. I hope he will not keep it under consideration as long as he has the appointment of a trade commissioner to Cuba. He should appoint to Cuba, the best man he can get, and he should also give his personal attention to the matter I have just suggested, that is a measure of reciprocity with Cuba.

It is very unfortunate that a matter of this kind, that is a purely business question, cannot be discussed in this committee or in this House without party politics being brought in. I regret very much that the leader cf the opposition (Mr. Meighen), not only to-night, but on former occasions, and particularly to-night when there was no reason for giving the discussion that turn, should see fit to speak in the way he has. I made no attack on the Civil Service Commission beyond this particular question. I presume that the Civil Service Commission is capable of doing good work, of filling an important position in the country; but it is not capable, judging by results, of appointing trade commissioners, and it is hardly probable that we can get practical, useful, experienced trade commissioners under the system now established. The results show that. I wTas a little disappointed at the remarks made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), who knows a good deal about actual conditions of the Civil Service Commission. Under ordinary circumstances, for some positions, I believe the merit system, the system adopted by the Civil Service Commission and the examinations held by them, would give good results; but surely the hon. member for West Calgary will see that we cannot get results with regard to this question from the Civil Service Commission under present conditions.
Why not?

Because the best trade commissioner that could be sent from Canada to the West Indian islands or to Cuba, might be a man who could not pass the Civil Service examination at all, who would have no chance of being appointed under the present system. If my hon. friend were a business man, I think he wrould realise that.
Oh, oh.
I presume he is a capable lawyer, a capable man.

Do not make any violent assumptions.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

If he is not a capable man, a capable lawyer, I am sorry. I would presume thait much. I will agree with one remark made by the hon. member for West Calgary, that is that it would be practically impossible to get men engaged in active business to accept the salaries that are paid to trade commissioners. The salaries ought to be increased in order to get good, suitable men, because if you cannot get good, capable men, there is no use in appointing any one at all. The men who might be obtained would be men above forty years of age, suitable, practical, capable men, men who are advanced somewhat in years, who have perhaps, retired from active business, who have had wide experience and who would be ready to take a trip and a position of that kind for a few years. They are, in my opinion, the Very best men that could be appointed.

How much would you
have to pay such a man?

I do not know, but that man would take a smaller salary than a man about forty years of age who was engaged in active business, and he would be just as suitable and-capable at fifty years of age. The experience he had gained in his own business would be of great value to him. Another thing that should be taken into account in appointing a trade commissioner is that he should have experience in the business of the part of Canada that he represents. For instance, if a trade commissioner were sent to the West Indian islands or Cuba where probably seven-eighths of the business is carried on with the Maritime provinces, then a Maritime province man should be selected, who is especially acquainted with the business of that part of Canada. If he is wanted to represent business in which Ontario or western Canada is chiefly interested. he should be a man from that part of Canada. It is results that we should look for. American consuls in different countries are, I think, really trade commissioners; they are generally men somewhat advanced in years, while the tendency in this country is to send boys. It is no crime to be a young man, or to have a diploma from a university or to be a graduate from a university; but keep those men in the position for which they are qualified. In a large place, one of those young men might very well be 'an assistant, and in time to come, he might prove very useful. But I do want to repeat the observation so well made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). What man of common sense in this country would imagine that a
graduate from Edinburgh university who went to Winnipeg and was not a success at law, although perhaps useful in other respects, could be of any use at all in Cuba as a trade commissioner? That is the kind of result you get under the present system. I do not, want the leader of the opposition or anybody ellse to say that we are attacking the Civil Service Commission. I am not doing so at all events, but I repeat the statement that under the present system it is a farce for the Civil Service Commission to make appointments in this particular work. It is ridiculous and is a waste of money.

I asked the minister
some time ago to give us the exports and imports between Canada and Cuba on the one hand and Canada and Jamaica on the other.

The exports to Cuba last year amounted to $5,816,568 and the imports $8,992,490. That was for eleven months ending February 1924. In the case of Jamaica the exports amounted to $2,793,387 and the imports $2,949,232.
Of what did the imports and exports chiefly consist, between Canada and Cuba?

I have not the details. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) asked me whether I thought that the trade agents were paid an adequate salary. I can only say that in this case also the salaries are fixed by the Civil Service Commission, so that I have very little say in the matter. The hon. member expressed the view that a university graduate with a year's training in the -department was sufficiently equipped for the position of trade commissioner. I know that my hon. friend is recognized as one of the leaders of the bar in his province, and I would ask him the same question that I asked the leader of the opposition some time ago: does he think that a graduate from a law school, after a year's experience in a law office, would make a good judge for one of the high courts of the country? The hypothesis is analogous to the present case.

In view of the fact
that, as the figures which the minister has given show, our trade with Cuba is so much greater than it is with Jamaica, what excuse is there for the transference of the trade commissioner from Cuba to Jamaica? I venture to say that the trade between Canada and Cuba is capable of far more development than the trade with Jamaica, and the exports from this country to Cuba consist chiefly of potatoes while the imports from Cuba are made up almost entirely of sugar. I would

Supply-Trade and Commerce
impress upon the minister once more the necessity for the appointment of a trade commissioner in Cuba.
Mr. LeSUEUR:	We have this evening
heard a great many remarks about the inefficiency or the incompetency of our trade commissioners, and the blame has been placed upon the Civil Service Commission. I have failed however to see any specific statements or any specific proof which would connect these two things. If you are going to judge of the appointments made by the Civil Service Commission, of the efficiency of trade commissioners, or of the regulations under which the Civil Service Commission appoints these men, your first study must be of the duties which the commissioners are expected to perform. I ask the committee, what are the duties which Canadian trade commissioners in foreign countries are called upon to discharge? In the first place, they are supposed to have a fairly accurate knowledge of the products and manufactures of Canada which will be suitable to the particular country in which they are representing us. In the second place, I would assume that they would be expected to mix with the people of that country, to get acquainted with the buyers there, and then to supply them with the necessary information regarding Canadian products and manufactures. Furthermore, a very essential thing is that they should be men of address and of a certain culture who can become acquainted and stand in with those with whom they do business. These commissioners require very different qualifications from the mere ability to sell goods in Canada for a particular industry. The situation is absolutely different: it requires intelligence, a general knowledge of the products and manufactures of this country-although not a detailed knowledge of any particular line-and then energy and push, along with a certain address so that these men may be able to ingratiate themselves into the esteem of the people of the country in which they represent Canada. If, as I believe, these are the qualifications, then the remarks of the hon. member for West Calgary are very pertinent, and the investigation and examinations which he shows that the Civil Service Commission makes are indispensable to the choice of men suited for the business. I have been personally in very close touch with the commercial attaches of the United States, and with the representatives of Great Britain, in a great many of the southern countries; I know the duties which they are expected to perform, and I know that these are the qualifications which they require. When we speak of choosing a

man at the age of thirty-two we must remember that this is the age that is set for entering the service. A man is not supposed to enter the service one year and go out the next; he expects, I presume, to be entering upon a career. Such a man believes that he will ascend in the service, and naturally after having trained in the department for a year and a half or two yearn, during which time he has got acquainted with Canadian conditions generally, he goes abroad and takes a minor post and gets experience in his new location. At thirty-two a man's mind is plastic, his nature is not set, and he adapts himself to people more or less easily. Then, again, the psychology of the people in these foreign countries in which our trade commissioners represent us is entirely different from that of our own people; and it has been the experience of a great many of our manufacturers and our big business concerns that the travellers who have been sent out from Canada and the United States do not make the success in those countries which they achieve here for the simple reason that they do not understand the people. A man of thirty-two has certainly been out of college several years, and there is no reason to doubt that he has acquired a certain amount of experience.

Does the hon. member think
that a man of forty should be barred?
Mr. LeSUEUR: I was coming to that. I was saying that a man of thirty-two is plastic in mind, and he can more easily get into close touch with the people of a new country and better understand them than can an older man. Now, a successful business man at forty is not likely to be jumping into a trade com-missionership. The man of forty who seeks such a position does so because he has been a failure in business or for reasons of health, but in any event he is not seeking it as a career. If thirty-two is too inelastic an age limit, why not change the regulations? But I am putting that forward as the possible reason for the limit. As regards the Civil Service Commission, I do not see why they are not completely fitted to choose men with those qualifications. If our trade commissioners are not giving effective service, I believe it is due to the instructions they receive or to the way they are handled. As the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) very properly said, they are tied down too strictly, they have not sufficient freedom. A trade commissioner who cannot move out of his office to get after business when he sees it, who cannot spend a certain amount of money in maintaining his status and getting in touch with

Supply-Trade and Commerce
people, cannot of course be expected to secm-e results. It is the system and the organization surrounding trade commissioners more than their selection and appointment that I believe is at fault, if fault there be.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to correct an impression that possibly might grow out of the remarks made by the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member who has just taken his seat, to the effect that a certain trade commissioner was not allowed to travel over his constituency, as it were, without authority from the Civil Service Commission at Ottawa. That may be true in an isolated case, but as a matter of information I propose to give the committee a few items which I have taken from the Auditor General's report during the last few minutes. I find the following set out as the travelling expenses incurred by our trade commissioners overseas; $467; $336; $1,357; $4,057; $1,031; $2,085; $352; $271; $397; $2,846; $2,918; $1,636; $2,791; $2,472; $1,230;	$424;	$13,809. They total
approximately $40,000. Evidently some of these trade commissioners have been stepping out.
How many trade commissioners are representing Canada in the central states of the United States?
We have only one trade commissioner in the United States. He is located in New York.

Our trade commissioners over there seemingly have lost the market for us in cereals in that we have now to overcome a forty-two cent per bushel duty on our wheat. I do not know whether that reflects upon the hon. gentleman in that he was an appointee of the former administration, but we, in common with practically all countries, erect tariff barriers and then appoint trade commissioners to regain the trade which we have obstructed by these artificial barriers. I merely interject this remark to emphasize how unnatural it is that we should incur expense to undo the very thing we have done.
Are these trade agents appointed to furnish information to the Customs department?
No, but I am sure they would be very glad to furnish any information that the Customs department might ask for.

Are they used specifically
for that purpose?
No, they are not.

In view of the varied conceptions of what trade commissioners are supposed to do, perhaps the minister as head of the department can tell the committee precisely what are the functions of a trade commissioner?
To my mind a trade commissioner is simply a glorified salesman.

With all due respect and
humility, I submit that the minister has an entire misconception of- what a trade commissioner is. Like my hon. friend from Cumberland, I have done some travelling, and I have found that the British trade representatives in Italy and the other countries of Europe do not regard themselves as glorified salesmen. A trade commissioner cannot possibly be a salesman because he cannot be expected to have specific knowledge of every article manufactured in any country. My conception of his function is that he brings in contact the people of one country wishing to do business with the people in another country, and then their respective experts do the actual business. If the minister is of opinion that a trade commissioner is a glorified salesman it is little wonder that he and his followers are disappointed with the results obtained and wish to institute some kind of patronage system in connection with the appointment of these commissioners. I think the committee will be disappointed in the minister's conception.

The hon. gentleman apparently does not understand anything whatever about the functions of a trade commissioner of this country whom he is mixing up with consular agents and ambassadors. As the minister says, our trade commissioners are men sent to secure trade. When any of our trade commissioners are 'brought back, to Canada from time to time, as Mr. Ross is just now, they visit our manufacturing centres and get in touch with our manufacturers to see what they have to sell. In the Commercial Intelligence, published by the department, will be found a list of articles which any particular country desires to buy or sell.	-

Does the hon. gentleman
know the functions of a British trade representative in foreign countries?
Yes.

Does he assist there as a
salesman?

No. But conditions are entirely different in Europe from what they are in the West Indies. We are endeavouring to secure trade between buyer and seller, and our trade commissioners come between the two.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Does the hon. member suggest that the manufacturer of a special line of machinery in Canada would send to our trade commissioner in Cuba and get him to sell that machinery?
Why, certainly, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman has been asleep! If he reads the Commercial Intelligence he will find that that is being done all the time.

I think my hon. friend
has been at sea!

I have been at sea, but
not overseas.
Mr. LeSUEUR: Are there any trade commissioners in any country that do the actual selling of goods? Their duty as I have always understood it, is to bring the producer in touch with the buyer, but not to make the actual sale.
The hon. member is right. Our agents do not do any selling; they simply bring the buyer and the seller together.

Are additional offices to be opened this year?
Mr. LOW.: Some may be opened during the course of the year, but nothing has been definitely decided.
I understand that the position of director has been abolished and the occupant of that office sent to the West Indies. That should make a saving instead of an extra expenditure should it not?
The office has not been abolished, but the director has been transferred to Barbados.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is the vote that
was allowed to stand before six o'clock.

This employment service is
undoubtedly doing very valuable work in regulating the distribution of labour, particularly that variety of labour which is engaged in seasonal employment. I haVe before me, as illustrative of what I am referring to, the figures indicating the movement of farm labourers to and from western Canada during
1923.	In the spring and harvest seasons 5,519 men were transferred from British Columbia to the prairie provinces, and of that number 2,963 were subsequently returned to British Columbia. During the harvest season 34,599 harvest hands were transported from eastern
[Mr. Logan. 1
Canada to western Canada and of that number 29,021 returned to eastern Canada. Then, of British harvesters 11,883 were brought to western Canada; 1,385 returned to eastern Canada, and 2,284 to Great Britain; 225 were deported, and there remained 7,939, so that the estimated increase of farm labourers remaining in western Canada following the 1923 movement totalled 16,073, according to the figures. The work of transporting these men from British Columbia and from eastern Canada to western Canada during the spring and harvest seasons was largely, as I say, done by this employment service, and in order to see that the work is properly coordinated it is essential that it be continued in their hands. But there is another organization, the Land Settlement branch, attached to the Immigration department, which is engaged in bringing farm employees and labourers from overseas. The work of that branch has interfered very seriously with the work of the employment offices, and as a result of there being no co-ordination between the activities of those two departments there is a considerable amount of unemployment in various parts of Canada even to-day. I have noticed resolutions passed by the town council of Sarnia, by one or two other cities in Ontario and by some cities in western Canada, complaining of this unemployment and of the failure of the federal government to assume the responsibility. I suggest simply that it should be the minister's aim to endeavour to co-ordinate the work of this Land Settlement branch and that of the employment service with a view to seeing that there shall be no overlapping and that no injustice is done either to the employers of labour or to the employees themselves, especially those engaged in seasonal employment.
I think the minister was going to give me some information regarding the possibility of the establishment of unemployment insurance-what is being done in other places.

During the interval since six o'clock I have tried to get that information, but the file clerks in the department had gone home; consequently my hon. friend will have to bear with me until I can go into the department in daylight. I will get the information.

Oh well, I will not inquire further. The minister will not have anything to do with renewing it.
You cannot tell.

Item agreed to.
Administration of the Act respecting Annuities for Old Age, $25,000.
Will the minister say what progress his department has made toward establishing old age pensions? Could he give us an illuminating address on the subject?
There is a special committee of the House appointed to consider that matter.

The minister would be
on that committee?
' Mr. MURDOCK: For some reason, my name is not on the committee, but the committee is splendidly equipped to go thoroughly into the matter, and I shall be glad to give it any advice and assistance I can.

I think I could guess the reason why the minister is not on the committee, especially as the committee was moved by the Prime Minister. I think the chief reason would be that he does not want to be on.
I did not ask to be left out.

No, I do not think the request would be necessary; it probably was suggested to him that that would be the part of wisdom. How is it that the government has not made any progress with the subject? I would have thought from the prognostications of the Liberal campaign programme and from the known convictions of the minister, that we would be far on now with the subject of old age pensions. I am naturally interested in the question; I am approaching that stage myself, as is the minister, and I would not like to have a committee appointed session after session, merely as a means of shunting this question over from year to year. Has the government got nothing done? Has it nothing to lay before the committee? What is the government's idea of what an old age pension ought to be, and at what age ought it to start? How much is it going to cost?
How many questions are you going to expect me to remember and answer?

The minister can remember all these; if he is sincere, he must have been thinking of all these for years. Before going
any further, I would like 'to know what the minister can do in answering these I have already suggested.	.

The government has been very busy for the past four weeks dealing with a number of very important subjects. There was the long debate over the budget, for instance, and there have been many other very important questions, possibly no more important than the question of old age pensions, but questions that appeared to have priority having regard to the financial condition the country is in. I can assure my right hon. friend that the question of old age pensions has not been overlooked, but it is realized, as my right hon. friend will realize, that with the enormous financial obligations this country has to face, it cannot take too hurriedly upon itself an old age pension scheme that would entail a very large responsibility, without full investigation as to what it might involve. That is now being undertaken, and all in reasonably good time, not too hurriedly, and with due regard to the financial position of the country, it is hoped that something will be definitely recommended to parliament. Further than that I cannot give my right hon. friend any information except that the matter has been very carefully considered and will be carefully considered.
This is not beyond the jurisdiction of the federal authorities?
It has not been so ruled by the Justice department so far as I know.

My hopes are slowly sinking. Apparently the government have been giving very thoughtful and prayerful consideration to this question, but they have not got any further; they have not reached any views. Something is going to be submitted, some time, somewhere; the trouble is the country has a large debt, and consequently we must go slow in this thing. It is amazing that that idea did not enter the minister's mind in 1919. It is also amazing how it escaped his mind in
How do you know that it did?
It escaped in 1921.
In what way?
Because the minister did not make any statement to the country to that effect.
What statements did the minister make in 1921?

He made a lot he should not have made.
Supply-Labour

My right hon. friend
cannot point to one statement I made in 1921 on the subject of old age pensions.

No, I am complaining
that he should have. He comes now and tells us: We have to be very careful; we have a large debt. Well, we had a debt in 1921, not quite as big, but pretty nearly, and he had a platform in his hand, promising old age pensions, and he did not tell the people then we could not do it. I say it is a wonder the idea did not enter his mind at that time. No progress has been made since, none at all; other things have priority. Perhaps he would tell the committee just what priority the Union club and the Scribe hotel would have over old age pensions, and why.

Would my right hon.
friend tell us his views on old age pensions? Does he think the government ought now to establish old age pensions, and if so, on what basis?

My view is, if you do
not think so, you should not say so.
That is safe, anyway.

That is a line of safety
that the minister did not follow, unfortunately.

My right hon. friend
cannot prove one word of that statement; he cannot prove a word of it. It is all in line with his beautiful inaccuracies, that is all.
Have I the floor or has the minister?
I am drawing attention to the fact that he cannot get away with that sort of misrepresentation with me. He is stating things that are absolutely and unqualifiedly false.
Nothing worse?

No, just that, and I
realize that it is all a part of the function that he thinjks he has to perform, but he cannot get away with it with me. The right hon. gentleman cannot point to one statement I made about old age pensions in 1919 or 1921. He is only trying to make a noise to convince the country that he is doing something. The statement that I have made is in accordance with the facts. The government is proceeding in an orderly and considered way, having regard to the financial load that the right hon. gentleman, his government and his predecessors left with the

country, to investigate this question of old age pensions. It may not be to the liking of my right hon. friend and his "special interest" friends but the government is doing fairly well.
If the minister has anything else to say I will gladly listen. I would rather listen to him than be talking myself.

There is a lot more,
and it is all due you.

If the minister is exhausted, I will interject a few thoughts. I thought I had made clear to him that I did not say he had made any statement in 1921, but he subscribed to a platform in 1921, a platform which promised action in respect of old age pensions. This is the statement I made, and' nothing more, and all the minister's hackneyed adjectives, drawn from his long experience in other spheres, will not produce much more than amusement in this House. I thought he had learned the lesson in the early days of his first session that that kind of spread-eagle oratory is some century or two out of date, and unless he has something really to say, the less noise inflicted upon the House of Commons the better. It was with some difficulty, I know, that his colleagues restrained his exuberance in the early days of his entry into this House, but they did it, and the discipline was certainly most beneficent. Why forget the lesson he was taught?
Now, 'answering the bon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), he wants to know my views. I have never expressed to the people of Canada the belief that we could enter upon a period of old age pensions. I never intimated that we had; consequently I am not now answerable [DOT] for intimations before this House. That is my position on the subject. I know the position the country is in, but I know the country was in virtually the same position two, three and four years ago. The contrast, of course, will appear to the Minister of Railways at once. But apparently the government has done nothing, except, of course, this very anxious thought they have been giving to the question. They have not got past the thought. Why the committee of the House? What is the idea? The government had ideas on the subject years ago; what has become of them? Are they dissipated? Why the committee of parliament now to furnish new ones? Why not let some come from the administration? Could the Minister of Railways and Canals give us any idea of when

Privilege-Mr. Marcil
this something, at some time, is going to come before this House? I mean this proposal suggested by himself.

I have not said that
any proposal would come before the House. I hope that a report will come from the committee, a very ordinary method of dealing with all these affairs in order to get all the information requisite for parliament to form its conclusions. I do not know what proposals will be made, if any. I am in hopes that the committee will be able to report before the session is over and give us the benefit of the information they have received, as well as their deliberations in the matter.

Could the minister give
us his views-because we will respect his opinions, if he has any,

as to whether we should have these old age pensions?

My opinion is that we
should thoroughly investigate the matter before dealing with it.
